I APPRECIATE THE OPPORTUNITY to give a reaction to this thoughtful and sensitive paper. I am particularly struck, in reading the clinical examples, by the qualities of careful thought, dedication and delicateness in Dr. Horner's way of being in the therapeutic situation.

Nelson Foote  

IN THE WAKE OF WORLD WAR II—as we ominously go on terming it—Harry Stack Sullivan was captivated like others by the hope that his profession could help to prevent the recurrence of war and companion disasters like racism, political repression and religious persecution. He threw himself into this effort with characteristic energy, intellectual boldness and organizing ability. At the time of his death, he was pushing furiously into this forbidding territory. One of the several reasons for grief over termination of his brilliant flash across our mental horizon was that it halted the interdisciplinary expedition he was mobilizing to explore the sources of man's monstrous inhumanity to man. The figure of speech that comes strongly to mind is of President Thomas Jefferson dispatching Lewis and Clark to explore the Northwest Territory, with Sullivan in the role of Jefferson and this audience contemplating whether to attempt the roles of Lewis and Clark.

That the prospect of venturing into such territory is daunting no one should deny. While fools are ever ready to rush in with epithets in lieu of explanation, like calling malefactors "sick, " it is far from clear that psychiatry, even defined as broadly as Sullivan defined it, can claim already to have illuminated the wilderness of shared insanity. In his last few writings, Sullivan seemed less and less optimistic, but he pressed on bravely out of his commitment to do whatever can be done. I can think, however, as at the memorial meeting 28 years ago, of no tribute more fitting to pay Sullivan a generation after his departure than to fix our attention on the unfinished tasks he left us, among which this problem of how to relate the disorders of interpersonal relations with the disasters of social life around the globe is pre-eminent.

Three Aspects of Change in Adolescence

Anna Gourevitch

Anna Gourevitch

Anna Gourevitch
65 East 96th Street
New York, New York 10028

Anna Gourevitch  

THE PROCESSES THAT GOVERN CHANGE in adolescence form a complex pattern combining psychological, social and maturational factors. In this paper, case material will be presented to illustrate three aspects of adolescent development and their interrelationships: how the adolescent comes to grip with his identifications, how his experience of himself in the work gains in importance, and how he comes to reorganize his aggression as a necessary correlate of relinquishing juvenile forms of dependency. The fate of each of these developmental tasks depends to some extent on the other two, though change may occur in one area in advance of, or well behind, corresponding change in another.

The Problem of Identification

In the adolescent's search for a sense of direction, his parents gradually move into the background and he learns to rely more on himself and thus begins to realize his own strength. The adolescent who has not been prepared to assume responsibility may assert himself through rebellion. Or else he may put the blame for his failings on his parents and thus fail to see his own role in his difficulties. By reproaching his parents for, in effect, not having been ideal parents, he makes them responsible not only for the past, but also for the present.

Much of this happens internally and the adolescent is only partly aware of it. In the process we describe, the adolescent comes to terms with the problem of identification: thus, he learns to make choices and to deal with super-ego commands in such a fashion that they no longer are the orders of an irrational authority within him which is resented but must be obeyed.

I wish to acknowledge the invaluable assistance of Dr. F. A. Fluckinger in the preparation of this paper.

THE PEAKING OF INTEREST IN countertransference during the last ten years has many origins, not the least of which involves the growing awareness on the part of many analysts of the inevitability of countertransferential phenomena, and their inherent potential for elucidating the forces at work in each particular individual analytic setting. As is usually the case with scientific investigation, increased knowledge and understanding has led to ever increasing questions and puzzlement. Thus, the once prominent but unwieldy unitary notion of countertransference has given way to more refined ideas regarding the shape and nature of the variety of personal reactions the analyst may have to his patient. These newer classifications have raised additional important concerns, ones which Drs. Epstein and Feiner have attempted to address in the collection of essays they have edited entitled Countertransference: The Therapist's Contribution to the Therapeutic Situation.

Among the more frequently encountered countertransference categorizations are such distinctions as "subjective countertransference, " "objective countertransference, " "positive countertransference, " and "negative countertransference." Each of these classifications have in turn their own subdivisions, and it seems likely that with further study these groupings will spawn even more offspring. Such distinctions are useful when they provide a clarification of what is transpiring in the analytic situation, and thereby help to orient the therapist to a more efficacious position vis-à-vis his patient. They cease to serve a constructive purpose when they become armaments in a metapsychological polemic over what does and does not constitute countertransference. H. Jagoda-Michalski

H. Jagoda-Michalski  

To the Editor:

THIS COMMUNICATION CONCERNS A GROUP of survivors of the Holocaust who spent this whole period or part of it impersonating non-Jews. Contrary to the others these people changed their external identity consciously and purposely, motivated by their intense will to save their lives. Their actions were carried out under conditions of constant extreme stress due to mortal danger, and the physical need to exist.

The external appearance of a human being is a compound of many factors which include external physical features, movements, clothing, facial expression, way of speech, behavior, reactions to sudden happenings and to ordinary events, etc. The appearance may be modified by constant interaction between the subject and the surroundings; the basis being a motivation to fulfill one's needs. Similar examples of identification with the surroundings by adjustment of the external appearance are known in many areas e.g., the survival mimicry of certain animals.

It has been observed that among children of diplomats (or other professionals) of non-Asiatic origin, who have spent long periods in the Orient, and who were looked after by local servants and nannies, original features were modified and there appeared some features which made them resemble the indigenous population.

The motives for my patients' behavior derived from their struggle for survival in a situation of great stress. Most probably they passed through a process of thought and feeling resembling delusion to finally acquire behavior fitting their aims.

Welcome to Symposium

Earl Witenberg M.D.

Earl Witenberg

Earl G. Witenberg, M.D.
20 West 74th Street
New York, New York 10023

Earl Witenberg  

THE PLURALISTIC APPROACH TO PSYCHOANALYTIC theory and practice of the William Alanson White Institute has been evident from its inception in 1943. Its founders, Erich Fromm, Frieda Fromm-Reichmann, David Rioch, Janet Rioch, Harry Stack Sullivan and Clara Thompson represented diverse approaches to the study of psychoanalysis. One shared interest was their intense dedication to devising new approaches to the study and treatment of man. Clara Thompson was in the forefront of those who attempted to make an open-ended approach useful for different kinds of people.

Harry Stack Sullivan (1892–1949), whom we are commemorating at these meetings, is best remembered for the new understanding he brought to the treatment of what today are called borderline and narcissistic personalities, as well as schizophrenic people. He added to treatment a theory—a theory of interpersonal relationships. This theory was based on a new paradigm for the study of man in his development and treatment, which stressed that what could be studied, what could be observed by clinical observations was the field between the two participants. Everything else was inferential. And in this field were the participants as well as illusory others—all others from the past of the psychiatrist and patient. There was no tabula rasa in the field. This, then startling, observation in the tradition of the American philosophers, Royce, Peirce and Cooley, made it possible to explicate the significance of the actual participation of the analyst, hence of the actual life experiences of the patient. It restored a balance to the problems more traditional psychoanalysts had and still have with libido and instinct theory, which grow out of a tendency to characterize actual experiences and attitudes as "nothing but" repetitions of the past. It legitimized analysts' reactions to patients and enabled these responses to be studied so that they could be used for the benefit of treatment. Havens has characterized Sullivan as secretly the most influential of American psychiatrists.

Countertransference Issues with the Later Life Patient

Emilie Sobel

Emilie Sobel

Emilie F. Sobel, Psy.D.
40 East 89th Street
New York, New York 10028

Emilie Sobel  

KARL ABRAHAM (1919) WAS THE FIRST analyst to strike a note of optimism about treating the later life patient. He noted, however, as have many analysts who work largely with regressed elderly patients, that they wish to be "guided" by the doctor, who signifies "the superior father" to their unconscious. This characterizes the transference of the elderly patient. Magical expectations that the therapist be an omnipotent figure who is a safeguard against external danger dominates the relationship. The therapy does not aim at uncovering, insight or reconstruction, but seems to merely be a holding operation. The therapist thinks in terms of limited goals such as improved daily functioning and applies a limited form of treatment which falls into the category of brief or supportive psychotherapy.

Two types of countertransference difficulties arise in therapeutic work with the regressed later life patient. The first are those resistances which have to do with professional ageism, i.e. fear and prejudice against advanced age which is prevalent in our society. This type of prejudice leads to referrals and recommendations other than therapy, such as adjunct services or nursing home placements. It is commonly assumed that the regressed patient is senile and the regression is irreversible. Actually there is an emotional breakdown due to loss and other precipitating stress factors which overload the adaptive capacities of the individual during a period of life marked by declines of all kinds. This type of prejudgment masks the therapist's anxiety aroused by the loneliness, helplessness and death imagery that these patients evoke. A second type of countertransference difficulty, however, has to do with the nature of the modifications in technique which accompany the application of brief, supportive, transference indulgent psychotherapies. beyond the clear, unmystifying demonstration of the complex interplay between analytic listening and the patient's self-esteem: Dr. Chrzanowski shows us the actual molding of the therapeutic interaction. Instead of reasoning backward from a therapeutic triumph to the inevitable foundation on which it necessarily had to be built, Dr. Chrzanowski has disciplined himself to look first and fairly at how his perceptions and actions came about and how they were responded to. Such studies are as fundamental to the progress of our field as they are rare in the literature. They alone can provide something that can be considered data.

As data, they can be analysed in many different ways. Ultimately for example, they can be exploited for the theory of therapeutic action. My own interest here, however, is with the narrower question of the place and function of cognition in psychoanalytic listening.

That is a funny question, to be sure. After all, what isn't cognitive in listening? Nothing experienced in the consulting room is sharply separated from cognition. But there are gradations we are all familiar with. The analyst probably absorbs the scene through a spectrum of responses, at one end of which his grasp is spontaneous, affective, personal, and interactive, while at the other, it is deliberate, abstract, systematic, theoretical, and impersonal. At one end of the spectrum, situations are recognized by reacting to them, as when we adapt our hand to a cup, or get angry at an insult. At the other end, we think to ourselves about the patient, and call our registrations "cognitions."

But theory and thinking are not all at one side, nor affect and action at the other. There is a theory in every reaction. I will call it high-level theory at the cognitive end, and low-level theory at the affective end. By the same token, there is a vested interest in all reactions, no matter how theoretical, though at the cognitive end, the affect may bleach out as a mere sense of curiosity.

Introduction

THERE ARE A NUMBER OF REASONS why converging views in psychoanalysis do not blend easily. One apparent barrier to productive interchange among analytic schools of thought is that each has to uphold its own deeply ingrained doctrine. I admit to a psychoanalytic anti-parochialism which is based on my conviction that dogma and personality cults do not promote clinical progress. I consider Harry Stack Sullivan to be among the relatively few genuine innovators in a field that was crafted by Freud's genius. Despite psychoanalysts having tended to be vigilant guardians of territorial boundaries, there is a legitimate need today to incorporate the growing body of empirical data in the overall theory and practice of psychoanalysis.

Experience has shown that open-ended discussions about the merit of one theoretical system over another do not lead to a consensus. More often than not people arrive at a restatement of their formerly held belief systems. A belief is a commitment to something that is beyond proof. It is usually the compulsive adherence to the truth of one's belief that gets in the way of considering another point of view. Psychoanalytic theory functions similarly to the phenomenon of an introject, that is as an internalized common belief system among a group of people who derive their professional identity from it.

Theory and practice in psychoanalysis represent complementary aspects without necessarily being in accord. The actual analytic work with the patient requires a theoretical framework as does the teaching of analytic therapy.

John Schimel  

The Physician

A MAJOR CONCERN OF HARRY STACK SULLIVAN was to capture in language the world that is there, the palpable world, the world that one can hear, the world that one can touch, taste and smell, a world that one can imitate and point to and repeat. It should be a world in which the behavior of his patient evokes in the psychoanalyst that which he himself has experienced, come to recognize and understand, and eventually to forgive and even love in himself. There are other worlds, worlds that are not here or there or anywhere, created by the misuse of thought and language, worlds occupied by some psychoanalysts and certainly by their patients, whose misuse of thought and language must be a matter of central concern, since the patient's thought and language are not only pathognomonic in regard to his emotional disturbance but also because change in the patient's thought and language is the best index of favorable change in his emotional condition and functioning. Sullivan's focus on the here and now transactions of patient and psychoanalyst, necessarily interactional and primarily conversational, attests to his concern with the observable and classifiable and ultimately the scientific appraisal of the immediately available data. In this he was following the principle of parsimony, assembling his data and making the most economical of explanations that could embrace the available information. From this guiding principle there emerged the only rational theory of psychotherapy, as opposed to theories of personality, that is available to psychoanalysts. In the course of this paper, I will try to demonstrate why I believe this is so. I sometimes think of Sullivan's approach as the application of formal logic and epistemology to the realm of human affairs.

Gloria Friedman  

TODAY WE LOOK UPON the mother-daughter relationship sensing that we have new discoveries to make. There still seems to be something illusive about the issues of female development. At times we wonder if some of the problems of our women patients—their dependencies, depressions, inhibitions—are an assignment by the culture. But psychoanalysts are not content with such explanations.

I believe that there is something in the separation and identification process between mothers and daughters that makes the daughter's struggle for independence and sense of herself as a woman so difficult to achieve. While I have become impressed with a number of significant aspects of the mother-daughter relationship, in this paper, I would like to focus on what I believe is an essential factor in the successful emergence of the adult woman, namely, the establishment of a loving bond between mother and daughter.

In addition to their maternal, nurturing roles, one major task that mothers have, is to hand down a legacy of womanhood—to teach it, cultivate and nurture it, and especially to share it and be an example of it. This is the message from mother to daughter about what it is to be female.

A painful aspect of this task is for the mother to facilitate the separation process—to stand back and permit it to happen—in fact, to encourage it. Too often we overlook the pain involved for both mother and daughter as they struggle to become independent of each other. I am not referring to the anxiety activated by the separation process, but to the anticipation of loss and change, and the painful awareness of this by the dyad. Others have also described the mother's experience of loss. Deutsch (1944) noted that the mother often felt abandoned by her adolescent daughter. IN MY BOOK (HORNER, 1979) I HAVE attempted to bring together attachment theory, cognitive theory which deals with mental structures, and object relations theory. The major focus is on the evolution of a cohesive, reality-related, object-related self. This self develops within the context of the maternal matrix, and the primary mothering person is viewed as the mediator of organization. Analogously, psychotherapy (or psychoanalysis) is conceptualized as a therapeutic matrix within which the therapist is similarly seen as the mediator of organization. My approach can be understood as a theory of the self. The shift fom classical psychoanalytic drive theory to object relations or self theory is completed with the position that instinctual drive is only one aspect of experience which must be integrated within the self-representation along with other aspects of experience, whether they be of internal or environmental origin.

I will first present an overview of early development and its consequences with respect of character structure. Following this, I will address the issue of the psychoanalytic treatment of patients with character disorders, with defects or deficits in the structure of the self.

The Object Relations Framework

The development of object relations has become increasingly central to present day psychoanalytic theory. The work of Margaret Mahler (1968), (Mahler, Pine and Bergman 1975) on the separation-individuation process in particular, has played a major role in this shift in emphasis.

The Psychoanalytic Dilemma

DAVID RAPAPORT (1951, P. 161) IN discussing Piaget's theory of mental development as a psychoanalytic paradigm, laments that "… the significance of communication in particular, and interpersonal relationships in general, for the development of human thinking, has been little appreciated and less explored." Harry Stack Sullivan, Rapaport asserts, is one of the few people who "… had a clear perception of this significance. … Sullivan coined the concept of 'consensual validation' to say that concepts and thinking become reality adequate only by being tested in interpersonal communication."

Piaget (1932, p. 64) provided a connecting link in his statement that "… between autism and intelligence there are many degrees, varying with their capacity for being communicated. These intermediate varieties must therefore be subject to a special logic intermediate between the logic of autism and that of intelligence." The significance of this fact in understanding the therapeutic process in psychoanalysis implies the existence of a field of communication within which the organization of thought moves from a more or less autistic level to a level of greater rationality. The quality of that field can itself be examined as a variable.

This essay is part of a continuing series of informal symposia concerned with the theoretical and technical concepts of Harry Stack Sullivan.

Joyce McDougall  

SUMMARY

This paper has attempted to explore the eventual links between psychosomatic and hysterical symptoms in psychoanalytical patients. It is a continuation of earlier research (McDougall 1980) in which the difference between the two types of symptomatology was examined in some detail. In that paper I had proposed that psychosomatic phenomena, in contrast to hysterical ones, were devoid of repressed fantasy content capable of being verbalized and thus had no direct symbolic meaning such as we find in the unconscious structure behind neuroses. I came to question this concept of a total lack of symbolic significance, in the course of discovering the massive measures that certain patients employ in order to render psychic pain inoperative through a radical elimination of any representation of intense affect. However I was unable at that time to appreciate the underlying archaic significance of psychosomatic reactions to psychic conflict and to understand the economic impact that this entailed for the psychic structure.

Certain patients reveal in analysis that they have at their disposal few psychic defenses against mental pain other than total foreclosure

456

from the psyche of incompatible ideas, frightening fantasies and perceptions, conflicting instinctual impulses and painful emotional states. The lack of neurotic symptoms in such analysands frequently creates the impression of a stable and markedly "normal" personality structure. While it is true that everybody possesses a certain "psychosomatic potentiality" which readily reveals itself under conditions of psychic stress, these patients are more exposed to serious psychosomatic disorganization than those who have constructed neurotic barriers—or even psychotic ones—against psychic conflict and stressful circumstances.

In order to illustrate this theoretical conception of psychosomatic dysfunction I chose the case of a patient who had suffered for a number of years from varied psychosomatic disorders (gastric ulcers, asthma, tetany, cardiopathology). At the time of coming into analysis he was suffering from an extreme form of anxiety neurosis which was in fact an intermediate symptomatic phase between the psychosomatic phenomena and the development, under the impact of the psychoanalytic process, of neurotic symptoms (claustrophobia, obsessive concern with death, acute anxiety in social situations with other men, inhibitions with regard to travelling far from home and to looking at people or certain phobic objects …) This intermediate phase, characterized by overwhelming outbursts of apparently unmotivated anxiety corresponded to what Freud called an "actual" neurosis, a clinical category described almost exclusively in terms of somatic symptomatology; these symptoms were considered by Freud to have no symbolic meaning.

In the case of Isaac A., several years of analysis were able to reveal that his sexual relationships, although in appearance normal and satisfactory, were in fact profoundly anxiety-arousing, but he had no knowledge of this nor did he suffer from any neurotic symptoms or inhibitions that might have been constructed to deal with such anxiety. The anxious fantasies that came to light, while they did not exclude oedipal conflict and phallic castration anxiety, were principally concerned to ward off fears of imminent death, bodily disintegration and loss of identity feeling—psychotic rather than neurotic anxieties. As these archaic fantasies began to find verbal expression Isaac then started to produce neurotic symptoms. The psychosomatic manifestations and the anxiety outbursts concomitantly were markedly modified and disappeared completely for long periods of time … although, as the clinical material

457

shows, these symptoms would come back in full force when new conflictual material such as homosexual fears (and later, primitive sadistic impulses) came to the fore.

It is my hope that this psychoanalytic vignette has given some insight into the nature of the psychic economy that lies behind psychosomatic disorders and of the back and forth movement in analysis between somatization and massive anxiety states, and between these and the formation of hysterophobic symptoms. This clinical fragment also highlights the archaic sexual significance and primitive oedipal organization that may be presumed to underlie psychosomatic regression and other forms of acting-out disorders. When such symptoms are the principal ways in which stress and mental conflict are met, we are witnessing the result of defenses of a primitive kind that have been erected to deal with psychotic anxiety concerning body limits, ego identity and self-object confusions. It would appear that these have never been elaborated mentally and thus have not been able to be integrated at the phallic-oedipal level of organization; instead they have remained split off from the rest of the personality, but continue to exert their effect on mental functioning, with the result that many perceptions, larval thoughts and affective states fail to achieve psychic representation.

To characterize the psychosomatic phenomena that may result I have coined the term "archaic hysteria" to indicate that the conflicts concern early somatic libido or primitive sexual and sadistic exchange in which certain bodily zones and functions are confused with the mother's body or felt to be under her control. The capacity to represent psychically wishes and fears concerning primitive impulses depends on the earliest transactions between mother and infant. These will inevitably be profoundly affected by the unconscious of both parents, and more specifically by the place of the father in the mother's libidinal and narcissistic economy, and the role that her baby is called upon to fulfil for her.

I trust that the clinical illustration and theoretical reflections presented here may provide us also with further clues as to the hidden links between object libido and narcissistic libido. I am in disagreement with the theoretical standpoint which holds that there are essentially two libidos each evolving separately. Even though problems of a narcissistic order may dominate the clinical picture as they so often do in psychosomatic states, while object-libido relationships may appear to be problem free, it is my contention,

458

based on clinical experience, that the two forms of libidinal expression are always profoundly linked one to the other.

Finally I would reiterate that the so-called normal-neurotics (which we would suppose includes the majority of psychoanalysts) with today's longer analyses invariably come to reveal the sectors of their personality structure where there too, somatic symptoms, narcissistic problems, addictive behaviour, second-hand ideas and discharge in action have taken the place of psychic work—of thinking and of feeling. Thinking is a burden and facing one's feelings is frequently painful and humiliating. So we are not surprised to discover that we all have shadowy areas in our mental economy where we no longer take time to question ourselves and our motives nor seek to be in closer contact with our psychic reality.

OSCAR WILDE ONCE SAID THAT ONLY superficial people insist on looking beneath the surface; which is not as superficial a remark as one might think. For it is the surface that manifests all that is splendidly unique and idiosyncratic about biological life, from the butterfly to man. As Adolf Portmann pointed out, it is the principle of nature that the surface manifestations of an organism, its appearance, should be both colorful and unique and that its internal organs should be both colorless and commonly held. (Portmann, 1964). Psychoanalysis, in its maligning of the surface, of the manifest content, has become a process much akin to plucking a duck. It is true that bereft of our individual plumage we are revealed to be, as Harry Stack Sullivan (Sullivan 1953) commented, more simply human than otherwise; but we are also deprived of the highly idiosyncratic personal patterning that renders each one of us as totally unique and singular as our fingerprints.

I would like to develop this point, that uniqueness is neither a biological nor psychological frippery. From the early Greeks on, science has always dealt with communalities, with an attempt to find principles and rules, "laws" which govern and order natural phenomena. Aesthetics was permitted its eccentricities, but science was expected to conform to the canons of logic and reason. This paradigm of Newtonian clockwork order began to deteriorate with both Einstein's relativity and quantum physics.

POST-FREUDIAN PSYCHOANALYSIS IMPLIED a shift from a psychology of drives in which meaning was seen as appetitive and motivations were defined as functions of drives, to a psychology of self and character in which meaning is experiential and both motives and intentionality derive from meaning and the organization of experience. In previous communications, I argued that this shift implicated cognition, conceived as experiential knowing, as the core phenomenon of mental life rather than as an epiphenomenal derivative of drives as envisioned by classical theory. This paper will outline my views on character and self as derivatives of cognition, which I view as the central organizing factor in mental life. In essence, the notion of character or personality represents the general theory of cognition and its organization, while the self can be seen as a special instance of cognitive organization involving the transformation of experience into subjective meaning.

The post-Freudian revisionists of the 1940's, in my opinion, were re-confronting an early problem in psychoanalytic theory development. TERMINATION OF TREATMENT GENERALLY implies a cure. The physically ill patient, for example, usually stays in medical treatment until he is declared physically well. However, since cure in the case of psychoanalysis usually is defined in vague, abstract and ideal terms, it seems more fruitful to think about termination in terms of the patient's capacity to deal with his problems, rather than in terms of a cure. Therapy should help the person become more tolerant of himself through his understanding of the underlying meaning of his former feelings of shame, disappointment, discomfort, and anxiety. Searles (1965) has depicted the healing power of sustaining a phase of "pre-ambivalent symbiosis" with the patient, purportedly reflective of the primary matrix in which the early-most self arises. I SHOULD LIKE TO OFFER YET ANOTHER contribution to the already burgeoning literature on primitive mental states. LIKE MOST ANALYSTS MCDOUGALL has experienced a change in the kind of patient coming to analysis. The "good classical neutotic", if he ever existed, is becoming scarce. Severe character problems expressed through acting out are more common. Long analysis gives the neurotic time to find his psychotic dimension. McDougall also observed that the "good neurotics" with their so called "strong egos" are often inaccessible to the psychoanalytic process while others of more amorphous, narcissistic, projective structures, the so called "fragile egos" are able to make of their analyses fruitful and fascinating adventures for themselves as well as for their analysts.

Since these patients present such diversified symptomatology, McDougall eschews diagnostic terms. She does not believe that there is enough evidence for an organized entity called the narcissistic personality. In this book she describes and discusses patients with perversions, psychosomatic manifestations, narcissistic disturbances, acting out behavior. She calls them "the difficult patients." Through her experience of their powerful resistance to the analytic process, to which they seem nevertheless to cling doggedly, it became apparent that the character armor served the function of protecting their very psychological life, not simply their sexuality, as in the neurotics. For "the difficult patients" symptoms are used as a bulwark against overwhelming anxiety and pain in the face of the threat of dedifferentiation, loss of identity, the fragmenting implosion of the other.

Furthermore, these patients inevitably mobilize, in the analyst, his own psychotic defenses. He may be threatened by a loss of identity, his identity as an analyst.

A REVIEW OF HARRY STACK SULLIVAN'S role in the historical development of personality theory and the therapy of disordered living is long overdue. His influence can be recognized in every aspect of the behavioral sciences and his focus on the interpersonal elements in all human behavior, both individual and group, is especially notable in the burgeoning new theories that utilize the essential elements of communication or transactional theory. The relevance of his concepts can easily be identified in the Gestalt, Rational, Cognitive and communications theories as well as in the behavior modification approaches. It has been pointed out time and again that Sullivan is the secret agent who remains unacknowledged as the grandfather of these highly touted and so-called "original" developments in psychotherapy.

Sullivan's psychiatric theorizing was based on the contributions of early deviationists from Freud's psychoanalytic theory and therefore he had fewer preconceptions and entrenched and reified concepts of human functioning to undo than did his predecesors. His involvement was initially with the more severe clinical problems and although his earliest publications were in the traditional classical psychoanalytic mode, he soon abandoned the libido theory and the accompanying jargon, which he felt was inexact and tied to mechanistic, 19th century scientific philosophizing. His preoccupation with preciseness and his concern for definitions and formulations that were logically and scientifically sound required a new set of terms that unfortunately alienated many potential adherents. More significantly, these requirements interfered with his publishing and the only written legacy he left was an expanded set of notes called: "The Conceptions of Modern Psychiatry, " an incomplete autobiography, and a wealth of notebooks and recorded lectures which were transcribed and edited and form the basis of Sullivan's contributions to social psychology and psychiatry.

THIS PAPER WILL BE CONFINED to the subject of the receiving of gifts from adult patients during the course of psychoanalysis and analytic psychotherapy. The problem of gifts in relation to child patients is an interesting one deserving full and separate treatment. My discussion will deal with gifts in the common sense meaning of the term, as physical, palpable objects, things, etc. given as a present. The fact that a patient's verbal productions, dreams, secrets, etc. may be unconsciously perceived by him as a "gift" will not be dealt with here.

Freud (1917) remarked early

Those who question this derivation of gifts (from anal instincts and libido) should consider their experience of psychoanalytic treatment, study the gifts they receive as doctors from their patients, and watch the storms of transference which a gift from them can rouse in their patients. (p. 131)

From this it is clear that Freud expected that analysts might from time to time receive gifts from their patients and that they might even, at certain times, present a gift to a patient. In this same paper he noted that, in the unconscious,

The concept faeces (money, gift) baby, and penis are ill-distinguished from one another and easily interchangeable. … For its faeces are the infant's first gift, a part of its body which he will give up only on persuasion by someone he loves, to whom indeed, he will make a spontaneous gift of it as a token of affection. … Defecation affords the first occasion on which the child must decide between a narcissistic and object-loving attitude. He either parts obediently with his faeces, "sacrifices" them to his love, or else retains them for the purposes of auto-erotic satisfaction and later as a means of asserting his own will. (p. 130)

Later (1933) he stated:

We have learnt, then, that after a person's own faeces, his excrement, has lost its value for him this instinctual interest derived from the anal source passes over on to objects that can be presented as gifts. (p. 100)

Silvano Arieti  

IN THE TOIL OF OUR EXISTENCE, we all confront daily our basic needs, aspirations, and troubles. In one way or another, we are all mendicants for love, searchers for new crumbs of truth, for a taste of softness and serenity, or for a patch of beauty. We do the best we can in our own petty, customary ways.

Although each of us tries to retain his autonomy and originality, all of us are very much influenced and to some extent molded by the environment in which we live. Although not conditioned like Pavlovian dogs, we are relentlessly subjected to repetition of stimuli, persuaded to follow beaten paths, to adjust to a routine.

A combination of chance events and of my own choices has made me become intensely involved with two groups of people who confront their basic needs, aspirations, and troubles in completely different ways, that is, by attempting to transform reality. These two groups, the schizophrenics and the creative persons, are both fugitives from the daily reality in which they feel prisoners. The ones and the others are shaken by what they feel is terribly absent in this world, and they send us messages of their own search, and samples of their findings, that is, of the transformations which they themselves have put into effect. But, some of you may object, the transformations of these two groups of people are quite different. The creative person wants to change reality in order to beautify it, or to enlarge the field of human knowledge or experience, in order to provide usefulness, understanding, and predictability, or to evoke a universal response. The schizophrenic instead is terribly afraid of this planet, of remaining close to the soil, this soil which will eventually bury all of us; but he has no wings to fly into high space. Empathy, Anxiety and Reality—A View from the Bridge

Philip Bromberg Ph.D.

Philip Bromberg

Philip M. Bromberg, Ph.D.
40 East 89th Street
New York, New York 10028

Philip Bromberg  

SULLIVAN'S NOTION OF "PERSONIFICATION" implies that the way a person relates to other people is a reflection of how "people" are represented mentally, how the "self" is represented mentally, and at what developmental level the concept of "relationship" is represented mentally. Further, and perhaps more important, it is the maturational level of the patient's representational world which determines the degree to which Sullivan's concept of consensual validation is possible as a therapeutic process, and thereby shapes one's analytic approach to any given patient. It is, in other words, the bridge which links developmental theory to the interpersonal method of participant observation.

In another paper I presented a structuralistic perspective of consensual validation (Bromberg 1980) which I suggested might allow the concept greater theoretical scope in accounting for therapeutic regression and the depth of change that we observe clinically in the process of psychoanalysis. I offered the view that as a necessary step, the developmental continuum of mental representation in interpersonal theory needs to progress beyond Sullivan's personifications of "good-me", "bad-me", and "not-me", and that the groundwork had already been prepared by Sullivan (1950) for subsequent elaboration, despite his own reluctance to take these ideas farther.

It has been suggested (e.g. Klenbort 1978) that a possible reason for Sullivan's hesitancy in doing so is that it would have required him to make a clearer distinction between the concepts of self, and self system —a distinction which was implied in his early formulation of self dynamism (Sullivan 1940, pp. 18-29) —and would have thus opened the door to the idea of unique individuality, a notion which he vigorously challenged. Reciprocal Aspects of Psychoanalytic Listening11

Gerard Chrzanowski M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski

Gerard Chrzanowski, M.D.
250 East 87th Street

Gerard Chrzanowski  

AT FIRST GLANCE LISTENING IS a commonplace phenomenon that does not deserve special consideration. A closer look dispels this impression and discloses a highly intricate manifold system of a transactional nature.

I addressed myself elsewhere (1978) to the epistemological tenet that thinking, listening and speaking, perceiving are not independent, self-contained phenomena. My emphasis was that all such processes are contextual in nature and cannot be isolated from the particular setting in which they occur. In the therapeutic situation the material coming from the patient is never projected on the therapist as a tabula rasa or blank screen, but rather onto a person whose way of listening in turn contributes to the ongoing patterning of communication. Psychoanalytic listening is definitely a two-way phenomenon. The analyst's attending attitude can either call forth or discourage the emergence of significant data related to the patient's self-image. The patient as speaker, the analyst as listener create jointly an atmosphere that, it is hoped, enables the patient to address himself to highly personal issues for which the analyst has a receptive ear. I also suggested that the construct of self-esteem may serve as a workable, empirical basis from which to obtain therapeutically useful data especially if the preconceived notion of psychological conflict as a primary cause of most cognitive distortions is transcended (Chrzanowski 1979a), (1979b).

Ted Saretsky Ph.D.

Ted Saretsky

Ted Saretsky, Ph.D.
Madison Street
Hewlett Neck, New York 11598

Ted Saretsky  

RECENT FORMULATIONS ON THE NATURE of the therapeutic process in the treatment of patients with borderline and narcissistic personality organizations, has focused increased attention on the psychoanalytic setting as a maturationally facilitating interpersonal matrix (Winnicott 1965), (Langs 1974), (Giovacchini 1975), (Epstein 1979). Within this framework the analyst's capacity to successfully address himself to the patient's ego-splitting and projective tendencies and make corrective interventions are generally regarded as central to the strengthening of ego-boundaries and the development of a sense of separateness and significance (Guntrip 1971), (Kernberg 1975), (Saretsky 1977). From an adaptive point of view, there is a growing tendency to define transference as reflecting something more than simply the patient's repeated attempts to force the analyst to assume the role and function of some part of himself or of some internalized other. This departure from the classical conceptualization of transference takes into account the possibility that the analyst-parent is being offered a fresh opportunity to react in such a way that would have a positive, mutative effect on the patient's ego (Epstein 1979), (Searles 1975). Greenson (1967), Racker (1968), Klein (1974), and Feiner (1977) have suggested that the analyst's ability to meet this challenge, to contain, treat and transcend his raw countertransferential responses, is crucial in the determination of whether the patient can be helped to break away from familiar pathological self-object relationships.

Anna Gourevitch

Anna Gourevitch

Anna Gourevitch
65 East 96th Street

Anna Gourevitch  

I: Tension

REVIEWING THE PSYCHOLOGICAL reports of a number of patients who have consulted me through the decades, I was struck by how each report began with a statement about the high level of the individual's tension. This once more confirmed my impression that the motivation to seek analytic treatment comes from the experience of inner discomfort that lies beyond the individual's ability to cope. Granted this, it necessarily is part of the analytic endeavor to understand not only the nature of the current life stresses but also the underlying sources of vulnerability, that is, the ways in which the individual manages tension at the characterological level.

For clinical purposes, personality structure sometimes can best be approached in terms of how the individual organizes his response to tension, how he attempts to manage it or evade it, and how it affects his ongoing experience. This is rarely a simple or straightforward matter. In practice we find that the mechanisms involved are intricate and often elusive. In this paper, I would like to present material concerning three aspects of personality organization as it relates to tension phenomena: the degree to which a person is unable to master ordinary tensions, the ways in which unresolved feelings and conflicts constitute an additional burden on the personality structure, and finally, the manner in which excessive characterological tension leads to an inability to cope adequately with stress.

Harry Stack Sullivan and American Intellectual Life

Bruce Kuklick Ph.D.

Bruce Kuklick

Bruce Kuklick, Ph.D.
Department of History University of Pennsylvania
Philadelphia 19104

Bruce Kuklick  

THIS PAPER DOES NOT primarily concern itself with the justification, refinement, or usefulness of Sullivanian concepts. My purpose is not even so much to trace the evolution of Sullivan's ideas as to locate them in the currents of American intellectual life of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In so doing I do hope that some of Sullivan's concerns and attitudes will become more comprehensible.

There are two developments I want to speak about at length. The first of these is what I call the naturalization of idealistic self-realization ethics in academic circles in the United States, and I'm going to spend some time explicating what that phrase means.

In post-Civil War America, absolute idealism was the conventionally accepted viewpoint among philosophers and theologians. Reality, they claimed, was ultimately spiritual and mental in nature; the physical world was somehow a part or aspect of an absolute consciousness, and sentient beings were finite, fragmentary, and partial embodiments of this spirit. Most commentators have lost sympathy for this doctrine, but we should not underestimate its respectability in the nineteenth century. It had an influential and impeccable lineage in Kant and the post-Kantians, especially Hegel; and it successfully made its way from Germany to Great Britain in the middle of the nineteenth century and, slightly later, to the New World. Moreover, while absolute idealism was obviously attractive to thinkers as a religiously oriented antidote to popular materialism, we need also to remember that it was simultaneously intellectually credible—idealism had sophisticated answers to complex questions in epistemology and metaphysics that had brought British empiricism to a dead-end in David Hume.
